== Introduction ==
Taylor mentions three types of secularity

# Secularity as Public Spaces: This sense of secularity refers to the separation of religion from public institutions and practices, especially the state. In a secular society, political structures are independent of any religious institutions, and religion or its absence is largely a private matter. This perspective also includes the idea that the "public spaces" of society have been emptied of references to God or any ultimate reality. The various spheres of society - economic, political, cultural, educational, professional, recreational - generally operate without reference to God or any religious beliefs.
# Secularity as Decrease in Religious Belief and Practice: The second sense of secularity refers to a reduction in religious belief and practice, implying that fewer people are believing in God, attending religious services, or practicing religious rituals. This sense is more related to individual and societal religious practices and beliefs, rather than the structure of institutions.
# Secularity as Condition of Belief: The third sense of secularity focuses on the conditions of belief, meaning the shift from a society where belief in God is unchallenged and unproblematic, to one where it is understood to be one option among others. In a secular society, belief in God is not the default or the norm; it is just one of many belief options available, and often not the easiest one to embrace. This sense of secularity speaks to the diversity and complexity of belief in modern society.
He argues going from a society of naive theism to naive atheism is the key thing. Westerners are naive atheists even when they are theists. The default has changed


Also of note is the distinction between religion as one of many possible beliefs vs religion as something people just believe in in a Christian pagan synthesis as their reality.


He defines religion with a Latin Christianity centric definition as the transcendent-immanent distinction.

== Chapter 1 bulwarks of belief ==
One important part of the picture is that so many features of their world told in favour of belief, made the presence of God seemingly undeniable. I will mention three, which will play a part in the story I want to tell.

# The natural world they lived in, which had its place in the cosmos they imagined, testified to divine purpose and action; and not just in the obvious way which we can still understand and (at least many of us) appreciate today, that its order and design bespeaks creation; but also because the great events in this natural order, storms, droughts, floods, plagues, as well as years of exceptional fertility and flourishing, were seen as acts of God, as the now dead metaphor of our legal language still bears witness.
# God was also implicated in the very existence of society (but not described as such—this is a modern term—rather as polis, kingdom, church, or whatever). A kingdom could only be conceived as grounded in something higher than mere human action in secular time. And beyond that, the life of the various associations which made up society, parishes, boroughs, guilds, and so on, were interwoven with ritual and worship, as I mentioned in the previous chapter. One could not but encounter God everywhere. 
# People lived in an “enchanted” world. This is perhaps not the best expression; it seems to evoke light and fairies. But I am invoking here its negation, Weber’s expression “disenchantment” as a description of our modern condition. This term has achieved such wide currency in our discussion of these matters, that I’m going to use its antonym to describe a crucial feature of the pre-modern condition. The enchanted world in this sense is the world of spirits, demons, and moral forces which our ancestors lived in.

==Chapter 2==

==3 The Great Disembedding==
Really short chapter

The excerpt discusses three primary forms of disembedding, all of which are crucial for the formation of modern individualism. These are:

# Disembedding from the cosmic sacred: This refers to the shift away from viewing oneself as part of a larger, sacred cosmic order, where one's actions, roles, and identity are intrinsically tied to the cosmos' spiritual and natural forces. This shift is complete and affects all people, unlike in earlier post-Axial moves.
# Disembedding from the social sacred: This involves a shift away from defining oneself primarily through social roles and community membership, such as being a father, a son, or a member of a particular tribe. This process is linked to the development of a "buffered identity," which emphasizes personal beliefs, individual experiences, and relationships with God.
# Disembedding from God as designer: This third disembedding posits a new relationship with God, conceiving Him as a designer. However, the author also notes that this understanding of God becomes eventually optional or "dispensable" because the moral order designed by God can be interpreted as promoting ordinary human flourishing.

These forms of disembedding do not necessarily occur sequentially or independently. They are interconnected and influence each other, contributing to a complex process through which modern individualism has emerged.

=== Social sacred ===
The "law of the people" and the "cosmic order reflected in the social order" represent two integral aspects of the social imaginary in pre-modern societies.

# The law of the people: This typically referred to the rules, norms, and standards that governed the behavior of people within a community. They were an integral part of social functioning, establishing expectations and guidelines for interpersonal relationships, responsibilities, and roles within the community. These laws served as a form of social contract, ensuring order and stability within the community. The law of the people has origins in Indo-European cultures, where tribal customs and communal laws were pivotal in maintaining social cohesion. Such laws were often orally transmitted and involved concepts of honor, kinship obligations, and mutual responsibilities.
# Cosmic order reflected in the social order: This idea posits that the social order of human societies reflects or corresponds to a broader cosmic or divine order. In many pre-modern societies, the cosmos was seen as a realm imbued with sacred forces and beings, and the patterns and laws observed in nature and the heavens were seen as prescriptive for human behavior. Hence, societal norms, hierarchies, and rituals often mirrored perceived cosmic orders, leading to a deeply intertwined relationship between religion and social structure. This concept is associated with a "porous" self, where individuals are seen as inseparable from their social and cosmic contexts.

Both these elements played significant roles in structuring society, establishing norms, and defining individual identities in pre-modern times. However, with the advent of modernity and the emergence of a more individualistic understanding of identity ("buffered self"), these elements became less dominant, leading to the disembedding processes discussed in your previous questions.

=== Points needing elaboration ===
There are several additional topics that were mentioned in the excerpt that haven't been summarized yet:<ref>https://chat.openai.com/c/240fa059-ec49-41ed-a61e-29692a94bd01</ref>

# Axial Spirituality and its Influence on Modern Individualism: The author talks about the Axial Age's transformational effect on society. The Axial Age refers to a period in ancient history when profound, new ways of understanding the self and the world emerged in multiple civilizations, which included the inception of major philosophical and religious movements. The author argues that the principles of Axial spirituality influenced the shift toward modern individualism.
# Christian Influence on the Disembedding Process: The author explains that Christianity played a crucial role in propelling this disembedding process, partly due to its emphasis on personal devotion and discipline, and its project of societal reform. Christianity introduced the concept of individual spiritual relation and personal moral discipline, thus distancing people from old collective rituals and identities.
# Weber's Thesis and the Protestant Ethic: The author refers to Weber's thesis about the Protestant ethic and its link to the development of capitalism. Weber's thesis asserts that the disciplined work ethic and frugal economic orientation within Protestantism, particularly Calvinism, helped foster modern capitalism.
# Buffered Identity: The author mentions the concept of a "buffered identity", an idea that points to a more inward, autonomous self that is less porous to social and supernatural influences than in premodern societies. This shift in identity perception contributed to the distancing from traditional collective identities and rituals.
# The "Corruption" of Christianity: The author uses Ivan Illich's phrase to describe how the original principles of Christianity were altered or "corrupted" over time, suggesting that Christianity's initial aim to establish a new kind of social order based on love and spiritual connection was eventually replaced by a more disciplined, normative society.
# The Connection between Spiritual Traditions and Social Forms: The author discusses how certain spiritual traditions are embedded within certain social practices, and how these relationships are often reciprocal and influence each other over time.
# The Idea of 'Subtraction Stories': This term refers to the view that modern individualism emerged simply through the erosion or subtraction of traditional social and religious restrictions, a perspective the author contests.
# The Shift in Moral Order Understanding: The author explores how our understanding of the moral order has shifted alongside the process of disembedding, framing this as a revolution in how we view the relationship between individuals and society.
